Text: Er Mu

Edited by Er Mu and Fanyu Meng

Boris Johnson, the British prime minister who floated the idea of “herd immunity,” tested positive for COVID-19 at the end of last month, and early this week his condition worsened and he was moved to intensive care. The epidemic in the UK really is getting worse. To lift the nation’s spirits, the Queen once again stepped forward and gave a televised address on the fight against the virus from Windsor Castle.

For anyone used to the American accents of Hollywood blockbusters, the Queen’s “Oxford” accent, Received Pronunciation, sounds refreshingly different. Some say American English is free and easygoing, while British English is reserved and aristocratic. Zhihu, the Chinese Q&A site, has whole threads debating which of the two to pick when learning English. Today’s topic is not which one is better. As far as Er Mu is concerned, language is just a tool for people to communicate, and any accent will do as long as you get your meaning across.

Today’s topic is how we produce sound, that is, how we speak. Some will say that’s easy: we speak with our mouths. True enough, but what does the full mechanism of voice production actually look like?

— You STEM types really do think in strange ways. Why on earth do you need to know how speech works?

— Er… no idea. For world peace?

Anatomy of the vocal tract

The figure above shows the structures we use when we speak. At the top is the nasal cavity. Moving in from the lips on the right, we find the tongue, and farther back, where the oral and nasal cavities meet, the velum (soft palate). Below that lies the pharynx, with the epiglottis on its right. Below the pharynx we reach the larynx, with the oesophagus on the left and the trachea on the right. At the top of the trachea sit the vocal folds, and to their right is the thyroid cartilage, which in men forms the Adam’s apple.

In 1960 Professor Gunnar Fant proposed the famous source-filter model to describe how we produce speech.

The source-filter model

The source is the vocal folds. The filter is the vocal tract, made up of the velum, tongue, nasal cavity, oral cavity and so on.

The vocal folds produce a sound with a certain spectrum. That sound then passes through the vocal tract, which acts as a filter and reshapes the spectrum, before it is finally radiated from the mouth. Different states of the vocal folds produce different raw sounds, while the position of the tongue, how wide the mouth is open and whether the velum is open or closed all change the characteristics of the vocal-tract filter. That is how we can make so many different sounds.

The source

The raw sound from the vocal folds comes in two kinds, depending on whether the folds vibrate.

In normal (voiced) speech the vocal folds vibrate, and the resulting spectrum is more discrete: a narrowband sound made of distinct harmonics.

[You can feel whether your vocal folds are vibrating by resting a finger on your throat.]

Spectra for different ways of speaking

When we whisper, the vocal folds do not vibrate. Instead, the sound comes from turbulence as air from the lungs rushes past them. The spectrum is then much richer: a broadband sound with only a weak sense of pitch. That is why you can’t sing in a whisper: singing needs changes in pitch.

These two kinds of sound correspond to voiced and voiceless sounds.

The filter

With the same source, a vocal tract shaped differently produces a different sound. The five key vowels, a, i, u, e and o, are made by changing how wide the mouth opens and where the tongue sits (front, middle or back). An important feature of vowels is that the articulators stay still while we say them, so their spectral features also stay constant.

The opposite of vowels are consonants. So how do we tell a consonant, and what characterizes it? When we say a consonant, the articulators move (closing or opening), so its spectral features change over time. The four plosives p, b, t and d, for example, all need the mouth to open suddenly.

In speech, vowels are often not that important: much of the time they don’t affect the message, which is why so many words reduce their vowels to a schwa. In singing, though, vowels matter a great deal, because a vowel can hold a steady pitch. That is crucial for singing, and if you don’t control it, you easily drift off-key…

The seven-syllable mantra “Burn my calories!”: the perfect test for spotting YCY (Yang Chaoyue, the Chinese idol famous for singing off-key)

To sum up: the state of the source lets us tell voiced from voiceless sounds, and the state of the filter decides whether we produce a vowel or a consonant. Combine the two, and that seems to cover every sound in English. Once you know how these sounds are produced, shouldn’t it be easier to adjust your own pronunciation and sound more native? In fact, many English-learning gurus recommend improving pronunciation by watching the mouth shape and tongue position of native speakers.

— Wait, who said earlier that pronunciation doesn’t matter?

— Er… looks like I just contradicted myself.

Let me stress again: accent really isn’t that important. The method above is just a little bonus from our “STEM nerds want to know why” series. Or, put another way, pronouncing things a bit more accurately makes it easier to communicate, which serves the original purpose of language.

— Phew, managed to talk my way back out of that, just about.

It also gives you another angle on how different English accents differ. Below are the tongue positions (horizontal axis) and degrees of mouth opening (vertical axis) for the five vowels in American English (top) and Australian English (bottom).

American English

Australian English

Italian English

Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HDZs0S7qd64

All the examples above are in English, but other languages work the same way. Work out where each sound of the Pinyin alphabet or the Japanese kana table is articulated, and your Mandarin or standard Japanese will probably come out fairly standard too.

Understanding this mechanism also helps explain a common saying: “Japanese is spoken at the front of the mouth, English at the back, and Chinese somewhere in between.”

Er Mu still wants to stress that language is just a tool for communication. As long as it doesn’t get in the way of understanding, an accent gives language meaning that goes beyond communication.

From the swagger of Northeastern “ni cou sa” (“Whatcha lookin’ at?”)

to the soft cuteness of Wu Chinese “hao fe la” (“Okay?”)

the “salt-and-pepper” tang of Sichuanese “nong guo cui zi”

the cheesy “plastic romance” of a Hunan-accented “let’s go see the yinfabuluo”

and the comedy of Hong Kong’s “I’m Zha Zha Hui” (actor Nick Cheung mangling his own name in a viral game ad), and so on,

we are not just exchanging information with people. We also get a feel for their lovable personalities, and even the history and culture behind them.

In 2016 Professor Joe Wolfe used 3D printing for a demonstration of the source-filter model. He built two artificial heads, one producing the vowel in “had” and the other the vowel in “heard.”

The voice-production demonstration

The first row shows the source in the time domain and the frequency domain. Both heads use the same source.

In the second row, the upper plots show how the vocal-tract radius varies along the tract for the two vowels. The lower plots show the impedance, which describes the “filtering” of the vocal tract. The impedance plots show four resonances (formants R1–R4) for the “had” head and five (R1–R5) for the “heard” head.

The last row shows the spectrum and waveform of the sound radiated from the mouth. The peak frequencies in the radiated spectrum clearly line up with the resonances in the vocal-tract impedance. The characteristics of the vocal tract largely determine the main features of the final sound in this experiment.

In reality, the sound that finally comes out depends not only on the source and the filter but also on how efficiently the mouth and nose radiate sound, and on the coupling between source and filter. We won’t go into the details here, because the greatly simplified model above already explains most of how the voice works and what it does.

One such phenomenon: why does inhaling helium make your voice go high, like Donald Duck quacking, while inhaling sulfur hexafluoride turns you into Thanos, deep and booming?

(I bet many of you have tried the first one. It’s a fixture at science outreach events, and you can try it whenever you come across a helium balloon. Just be careful.)

Speaking after inhaling helium and sulfur hexafluoride

Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JjJOS0BpgnM

Some will say this is because helium is less dense than air and sulfur hexafluoride is denser. That isn’t the root cause, though. The root cause is that the different gases shift the resonances (formants) in the vocal-tract impedance (R1–R5 and so on). Helium is less dense than air, so sound travels faster in it than in air. The formant frequencies are proportional to the speed of sound, so all the formants shift upward, and the pitch of your voice ends up higher.

Left: air. Right: helium.

Likewise, sulfur hexafluoride shifts all the vocal-tract formants downward, and the pitch of your voice ends up lower.
